title.en: The Sky-Facing Pot That Told the Time

summaryEn: Hoya discovers King Sejong's bowl-shaped sundials, set beside busy streets in 1434 with animal pictures so that people who could not read could still tell the time.
learningGoalsEn: Read and recognize 해 (hae, sun), 그림자 (geurimja, shadow) and the question 지금 몇 시예요? (jigeum myeot siyeyo?, What time is it now?).
Understand that the angbuilgu shows the time of day and the time of year from the sun's shadow.
Know that in 1434 sundials were placed beside busy roads and used animal pictures for people who could not read.
Know that Sejong-era sundials do not survive; the ones we see today were made later in Joseon.

origin.noteEn: Heritage history, researched from the sources listed on the Sources screen.

scenes.narrationEn: Hoya squints up at the bright sky. "In Korean, the sun is {kw:hae}," he says. "When the sun shines, things cast shadows. In Joseon, people used the sun's shadow to tell the time!"
scenes.captionEn: Hoya looks up at the bright sun
scenes.artBrief: Hoya shading his eyes under a bright sun, his small shadow stretching across the stone paving of a palace courtyard.

scenes.narrationEn: In 1434, in King Sejong's reign, a new sundial was set up. Its bowl was round and hollow, like a cooking pot looking up at the sky, so it was called {kw:angbuilgu}, the 'upward-facing pot sundial.'
scenes.captionEn: A bowl-shaped sundial faces the sky
scenes.artBrief: A bronze bowl-shaped sundial on four short legs, its open side facing a clear blue sky, a slim pointer inside the bowl.

scenes.narrationEn: A pointed needle inside the bowl casts a shadow. Some lines show the time of day, and other lines show the time of year. Where the shadow falls tells you both!
scenes.captionEn: A needle's shadow shows the time
scenes.artBrief: Close-up of the inside of the sundial bowl: a thin needle casts a dark shadow across a grid of curved lines; no writing or numbers.

scenes.narrationEn: King Sejong's sundials were placed beside busy roads, at Hyejeonggyo Bridge and in front of Jongmyo Shrine, so that people passing by could gather and see the time.
scenes.artBrief: A Joseon street scene: people in white clothes and a child gather around a sundial on a stone base beside a small stone bridge.

scenes.narrationEn: On King Sejong's sundials, the hours were shown with pictures of the zodiac animal spirits instead of letters, so people who could not read could tell the time. Hoya cheers, because the tiger, {kw:horangi}, is one of the twelve!
scenes.artBrief: Twelve small, friendly zodiac animals (rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, sheep, monkey, rooster, dog, pig) standing together in a circle on a grassy hill; Hoya waves happily at the tiger; no letters or numbers.

scenes.narrationEn: The sundials from King Sejong's time no longer survive. The ones we can see today were made later in the Joseon period, and several are designated Treasures, {kw:bomul}.
scenes.artBrief: Two elegant dark bronze sundials with fine silver lines, standing on cross-shaped bases inside a museum display case.

scenes.narrationEn: Some are kept at the National Palace Museum of Korea in Seoul. Hoya peeks at a sundial in its glass case and asks a museum guide, "{kw:jigeum-myeot-siyeyo}" That means, "What time is it now?"
scenes.captionEn: Hoya asks what time it is
scenes.artBrief: Hoya and a child friend in a museum gallery, looking at a sundial in a glass case; Hoya has a curious, questioning face.

facts.claimEn: The angbuilgu tells the time by the shadow the sun casts inside its bowl.
facts.claimKo: 앙부일구는 해가 만드는 그림자로 시간을 알려 준다.

sources.title: 보물 앙부일구 (Hemispherical Sundial)
sources.quoteOrLocator: "앙부일구(仰釜日晷)는 세종 16년(1434)에 … 만들었던 해시계로 시계판이 가마솥같이 오목하고, 이 솥이 하늘을 우러르고 있다고 해서 이런 이름을 붙였다. … 세로선은 시각선이고 가로선은 계절선이다. 해가 동쪽에서 떠서 서쪽으로 지면서 생기는 그림자가 시각선에 비추어 시간을 알 수 있다. … 24절기를 알 수 있다. 특히 세종실록에 글을 모르는 백성들을 위해 12지신 그림으로 그려서 시간을 알게 했다는 기록이 있어"

sources.title: 세종실록 66권, 세종 16년(1434) 10월 2일 을사 4번째 기사 「처음으로 앙부일구를 혜정교와 종묘 앞에 설치하여 일영을 관측하다」
sources.quoteOrLocator: 국역: "처음으로 앙부일구(仰釜日晷)를 혜정교(惠政橋)와 종묘(宗廟) 앞에 설치하여 일영(日影)을 관측하였다. … 구리로 부어서 그릇을 만들었으니 모양이 가마솥과 같고 … 신(神)의 몸을 그렸으니 어리석은 백성을 위한 것이요 … 길 옆에 설치한 것은 보는 사람이 모이기 때문이다."

facts.claimEn: Angbuilgu sundials were first set up in 1434 (Sejong year 16); the name comes from the bowl's shape, said to look like a cauldron (釜) looking up (仰) at the sky.
facts.claimKo: 앙부일구는 1434년(세종 16)에 처음 설치되었으며, 오목한 시계판이 하늘을 우러르는 가마솥 같다고 하여 이런 이름이 붙었다.

facts.claimEn: Inside the bowl, a pointer (yeongchim) casts a shadow on two sets of lines: hour lines and season lines (solar-term lines marking the time of year), so the time of day and the time of year can be read directly.
facts.claimKo: 시계판 안의 영침이 만든 그림자를 시각선과 절기선(계절선)에 비추어 보면 시각과 절기(한 해의 때)를 곧바로 알 수 있다.

verification.notes: Third independent pass. All quotes re-checked programmatically against fetched pages (Sillok, encykorea, 우리역사넷, NMK, KMA; KHS descriptions via the khs.go.kr open API SearchKindOpenapiDt.do?ccbaCpno=...). unesco.org/ich.unesco.org pages could not be fetched directly (connection reset); UNESCO wording and years (2009, 2013, 2018) confirmed from search excerpts of the UNESCO pages and KHS lists. Corrections: Heo Jun birth year dropped from narration/fact (sources conflict: 1539 vs 1546, encykorea internally inconsistent); Jang Yeong-sil rank sentence softened to match the Sillok ('decided to give'); 우리역사넷 added as second source for Donguibogam f4/f5; Ssirum UNESCO locator de-quoted.

authorNotes: Makers deliberately not named: KHS entries list different makers (1985 Treasure: 장영실·이천·김조; 2022-1 Treasure: 장영실·이천·이순지) and encykorea says the maker is unclear (citing the Sejo Sillok, 이순지 led instrument-making). The Sillok inscription says '神의 몸을 그렸으니 어리석은 백성을 위한 것' (drew the bodies of spirits, for ordinary people); KHS and encykorea interpret these as the twelve zodiac animal spirits; narration follows them. Omitted: KHS's description of it as Korea's first public clock ('first' claim); line counts (KHS 1985: 7 vertical/13 horizontal; KHS 2022-1: 15-minute hour lines), because they vary by instrument; the sundial returned from the United States in 2020 (KHS 2022-1). Surviving Treasures date from the 17th–18th centuries (KHS). Theme set to 'nature' (sun, sky, seasons, zodiac animals); BP04 places Sejong science under Pillar E, so 'crafts' is an alternative. REVISION: 'seasons' replaced by 'time of year' (KHS: 계절선; encykorea: 13 절기선). Scene 5 now says explicitly that the animal-picture dials are those of Sejong's time (encykorea notes later versions used written characters). The reading of 'drew the bodies of spirits (신의 몸)' as the twelve zodiac animals is the interpretation of KHS and encykorea, not stated in the Sillok inscription itself.
